The client problem: a software team already has a repository and wants a public web agent. Decide how Maritime should host that agent, what the team operates themselves, and which artifacts they need before they deploy.

market.summary: For a software team that already has a repository and wants a public web agent, the public pages point to Maritime's "Public web agents" flow: any repo with a Dockerfile at the root can be served on a public, no-login HTTPS URL, and Maritime builds it, runs it serverlessly, sleeps it when idle, and wakes it on the next visit (https://maritime.sh/docs/web-apps). The documented command is `maritime create my-app --repo https://github.com/you/app --public`, with `--repo`/`--branch` selecting the build and `--public` exposing the URL (https://maritime.sh/docs/web-apps). So Maritime should host the built container and the public URL, while the team operates the repo, the Dockerfile, and the app's own runtime behavior; the custom-container page frames this as wrapping the agent in a small HTTP server that speaks a two-endpoint contract, and notes that a plain web app with a public URL needs no chat contract (https://maritime.sh/docs/frameworks/custom). Before deploying, the team needs a Dockerfile at the repo root, a chosen branch, a port to expose (the `--port` flag is listed but its description is truncated in the source, so the exact default is an assumption), and a Maritime account/API key; signup requires Google, GitHub, or email plus verification, and the first machine asks for a card that is not charged during the free trial (https://maritime.sh/docs/quickstart). The CLI can log in via a browser code or, for CI, skip login and set `MARITIME_TOKEN` (https://maritime.sh/docs/cli). Pricing context: the first 7 days are free with up to $20 of usage (https://maritime.sh/docs/quickstart), and machines are billed per second, with agent boxes at $1/mo per 2 GB (https://maritime.sh/pricing). Note that these are public docs; the company did not commission this note.

insights.insight: The documented flow makes the Dockerfile the single most load-bearing team-supplied artifact, because it is the only place the team controls build and start behavior.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The docs describe a build-and-deploy flow driven by CLI commands against a repository, with the platform owning build and run. That means the platform executes whatever the Dockerfile declares: base image, dependency install, start command, and port. Every failure mode the team can prevent (missing dependency, wrong start command, port mismatch) lives in the Dockerfile, and every failure mode the platform surfaces (build failure, crash loop, unreachable port) traces back to it. Since the platform owns the build step but not the build recipe, the Dockerfile is the contract's hinge: it is team-owned input to a platform-owned process. Reading it any other way invites the team to assume the platform will 'make it work'.
implementation_ideas: Write a minimal Dockerfile that pins a base image, installs only runtime dependencies, and declares an explicit start command for the agent.
Bind the agent to the exact port the platform expects and make the port configurable via an environment variable with a documented default.
Add a health endpoint the Dockerfile's start command can be validated against, and test the image locally before the first deploy.
identified_risks: A Dockerfile that works locally but assumes host networking or a different port will fail at the platform's build or run step.
Unpinned base images drift and break builds the team did not change.
Start commands that fork or daemonize can confuse the platform's run supervision.
identified_opportunities: A tight, reviewed Dockerfile becomes a reusable template for future agents on the same platform.
Explicit port and health declarations shorten debugging because failures map to one artifact.

insights.insight: Branch selection is a team-owned deploy control, so the deploy branch should be dedicated and protected rather than the team's working branch.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The docs include branch selection in the deploy flow, which means the platform builds whatever branch is named. The platform owns the build, but the team owns which commit enters it. If the deploy branch is the same branch developers push to, every push is a potential production deploy and the public URL reflects unreviewed work. A dedicated deploy branch makes the deploy a deliberate act: merge to it, then deploy. This also keeps the contract clean, because the branch is a team-supplied artifact the team can gate with review, while the platform's build step stays unchanged. The risk is that branch protection and merge discipline are team processes the platform cannot enforce.
implementation_ideas: Create a dedicated deploy branch and protect it so only reviewed merges land there.
Deploy only from that branch and record the commit SHA alongside each deploy for traceability.
Add a pre-merge check that builds the Dockerfile so broken images never reach the deploy branch.
identified_risks: Deploying from a shared working branch ships unreviewed commits to the public URL.
Branch protection is a team setting; the platform will happily build an unprotected branch.
identified_opportunities: A protected deploy branch gives an audit trail from commit to public URL.
The branch gate doubles as a review checkpoint for agent behavior changes.

insights.insight: Sleep/wake and the public URL are platform-owned behaviors the team must design around, not configure away.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The docs describe sleep/wake and a public URL as platform responsibilities. That means the team does not run ingress and does not control URL naming or stability; it consumes them. The practical consequence is that the agent must tolerate a cold start: it should initialize quickly, avoid long boot-time work, and not assume warm state. The public URL is shareable but platform-named, so any external reference (docs, integrations) should point at the URL as an opaque value. Because these are platform-owned, the team's only lever is agent design: fast startup, idempotent init, and a health endpoint that reports readiness after wake. Assuming the platform will keep the agent warm or let the team rename the URL is the common misread.
implementation_ideas: Keep agent startup under a few seconds by deferring non-critical initialization until after the first request.
Make initialization idempotent so a wake after sleep does not double-apply state.
Treat the public URL as an opaque platform value and reference it from config rather than hardcoding a guessed name.
identified_risks: Long boot sequences make the first request after sleep time out.
Hardcoded or assumed URL names break when the platform assigns its own.
Non-idempotent init corrupts state across sleep/wake cycles.
identified_opportunities: Fast, idempotent startup makes sleep/wake a cost advantage for low-traffic agents.
Consuming the URL as config keeps external references stable across redeploys.

Over-labeling prudence as policy can inflate scope and delay deploy.
identified_opportunities: A tagged checklist doubles as a confirmation agenda with Maritime.
Staging dry-run catches missing artifacts before public exposure.

insights.insight: The platform/team boundary must be a written contract, not an inferred one: Maritime owns build, run, sleep, and exposure; the team owns repo artifacts.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Public hosting docs function as a contract whether or not they say so. Where the seam is implicit, teams fill gaps by guessing, and guesses diverge: some bake routing assumptions into code, others assume the platform handles auth. Naming each responsibility on both sides converts an implicit seam into an auditable one and makes the deploy manifest the single source of truth. This is the core of reading the docs as a hosting contract rather than a tutorial.

Add a docs section stating explicitly what the platform will never do on the team's behalf (auth policy, state persistence, secret management in code).
identified_risks: Teams infer responsibilities differently and mis-own the seam.
Implicit contracts couple the repo to undocumented platform behavior.
identified_opportunities: Boundary clarity becomes a differentiator and cuts support load.
A declared manifest keeps the repo portable and auditable.

insights.insight: A public web agent needs a documented sleep/wake and state contract, because idle-sleep behavior silently shapes agent correctness.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A public agent receives inbound traffic and may hold multi-turn sessions. If the platform sleeps idle instances, cold starts land mid-conversation and any in-memory session state is lost. The docs must state the sleep trigger, warm-up path, and where state should live. Without that, teams either over-provision to stay warm or ship agents that drop context. The contract should push session state to an external store and define a readiness signal so wake is observable.
implementation_ideas: Document the idle-sleep trigger, expected cold-start latency, and a warm-up/readiness endpoint the platform probes before routing traffic.
Publish a state-handling note: session state belongs in an external store, not process memory; show the hook point in the entrypoint.
Expose a wake/health signal in logs so teams can observe cold starts during rollout.
identified_risks: Cold starts interrupt live conversations.
In-memory state is lost on sleep, corrupting agent context.
identified_opportunities: Documented warm path makes public agents viable without over-provisioning.
Externalized state improves reliability and portability.

insights.insight: Public exposure is a shared responsibility: the platform owns TLS and routing, but the team must own auth and rate-limiting in-repo via documented hooks.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A public agent endpoint is an attack surface. If the platform terminates TLS and routes traffic but the docs are silent on auth, teams assume protection that is not there and ship open endpoints. The contract should state that exposure is public by default and that auth and rate limits attach at a documented hook in the entrypoint. This keeps security ownership with the team while the platform provides the transport guardrails, and it makes the exposure model explicit rather than emergent.
implementation_ideas: Document that endpoints are public by default and specify the auth/rate-limit hook point in the agent entrypoint.
Provide a reference middleware pattern for token auth and per-client rate limiting that teams commit to the repo.
Add an exposure field to the deploy manifest (public, token-gated, IP-allowlisted) validated at deploy.
identified_risks: Teams assume platform-side auth that does not exist and ship open agents.
Unbounded public traffic drives cost and abuse.
identified_opportunities: Clear exposure model lets teams own security with platform guardrails.
Manifest-declared exposure modes make posture auditable.

insights.insight: The deploy should be reproducible from a pinned branch with a root Dockerfile, so the public artifact always matches a known commit.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Maritime's public flow is CLI-driven, which means whatever is in the working tree at deploy time becomes the public agent. Without a pinned branch and a root-level Dockerfile, two deploys from the same repo can produce different artifacts, and rollback becomes guesswork. A root Dockerfile also removes ambiguity about build context, which matters when the CLI packages the repo.
implementation_ideas: Pin the deploy branch in CI config and refuse to deploy from any other branch without an explicit override.
Add a pre-flight check that fails if no Dockerfile exists at the repo root.
Tag each deploy with the commit SHA and record it alongside the public URL for rollback.
identified_risks: Feature-branch deploys silently overwrite the public agent.
A Dockerfile in a subdirectory causes an empty or wrong build context.
identified_opportunities: Every public deploy is traceable to a commit.
Rollback becomes a redeploy of a known SHA rather than a rebuild.

insights.insight: Port and token handling must be explicit and externalized: declare the exposed port, keep the API key in CI secrets, and inject MARITIME_TOKEN non-interactively.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A public agent is only reachable if the container listens on the port Maritime expects, and that port must be declared rather than inferred. On auth, the CLI needs an account/API key for CI and a MARITIME_TOKEN to run without an interactive login; both are credentials, so they belong in CI secret storage, not in the Dockerfile or the repo. Echoing them in logs is a common leak that turns a working pipeline into an incident.
implementation_ideas: Document the exposed port in the Dockerfile and in a repo-level deploy note, and assert it in a health check before switching traffic.
Store the account/API key as a masked CI secret and reference it only by variable name.
Inject MARITIME_TOKEN at deploy time from CI secrets and add a log-redaction step so neither token appears in build output.
identified_risks: Port mismatch between container and Maritime expectation leaves the agent unreachable.
Tokens committed to the repo or printed in CI logs require rotation.
identified_opportunities: Non-interactive auth enables unattended CI deploys.
Externalized secrets make key rotation a CI change, not a code change.

insights.insight: Write down the responsibility split before deploying: the team operates the image, app config, and secret rotation; Maritime hosts the runtime and public endpoint.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The client question is as much about who operates what as about artifacts. Maritime's public pages center on deploying a container via CLI, which implies the team owns Dockerfile hygiene and application behavior while Maritime owns the hosting surface. Leaving that implicit invites the team to assume Maritime monitors app health or rebuilds images, and invites Maritime to assume the team rotates its own tokens. A short written split, agreed before the first public deploy, closes that gap.
implementation_ideas: Add a one-page responsibilities note to the repo covering image builds, config, secret rotation, and runtime ownership.
Define an on-call boundary: team handles app errors and image rebuilds, Maritime handles endpoint availability.
Schedule a quarterly review of the split and of token rotation.
identified_risks: Unclear ownership of log retention and rebuilds after a base-image CVE.
Both sides assume the other rotates the API key and MARITIME_TOKEN.
identified_opportunities: Clear boundaries shorten incident triage.
The team can adopt stricter image hygiene without waiting on Maritime.

Because Maritime hosts a built container rather than source, the team can pin dependencies and freeze the runtime, reducing environment drif

insights.insight: The two-endpoint chat contract should be the only integration surface, and it must be schema-pinned before the container is built.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Maritime's public pages describe hosting a built container at a public URL, not a framework-specific runtime, so the team's server contract is the entire interface Maritime and users see. A two-endpoint design (start a turn, then stream or poll the result) is small enough to document fully and test locally, but only if request and response schemas, status codes, and error shapes are fixed first. Without that, the public URL exposes an ambiguous API and every client change becomes a redeploy. Pinning the schema also lets the team validate the contract with a local harness on the same port before Maritime ever sees the image.
implementation_ideas: Write a contract doc listing both endpoints, request/response JSON schemas, status codes, and error bodies, and commit it beside the Dockerfile.
Add a local contract test that runs the built image on the declared port and exercises both endpoints, including error cases.
Version the contract path (for example /v1/chat and /v1/chat/{id}) so schema changes are additive rather than breaking.
identified_risks: Schema drift between the doc and the server makes the public URL unreliable.
A two-endpoint design invites polling loops that multiply cold-start load if the poll interval is too tight.
identified_opportunities: A pinned contract becomes a reusable template for future agents the team ships.
Contract tests run in CI on the same image Maritime will host, catching regressions before deploy.

insights.insight: Port and bind discipline is the most common way a locally working container fails behind Maritime's routing.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Maritime hosts the built container and routes the public HTTPS URL to it, so the container must listen on the port Maritime expects and bind to 0.0.0.0 rather than 127.0.0.1. Local runs often default to localhost or a hardcoded port, which passes on a laptop and fails once the platform proxies traffic. Making the port a single env var with a documented default, and testing the exact image with the same bind address, removes the guesswork. This is a runtime concern the team owns, not something Maritime's public pages promise to fix for them.
implementation_ideas: Read PORT from the environment with one documented default and bind the server to 0.0.0.0 explicitly.
Add a startup log line that prints the bound address and port so deploy logs show the real listener.
Run the container locally with the same PORT value and bind rules the deploy will use, and assert reachability from outside the container.
identified_risks: Binding localhost makes the public URL return connection errors while local tests pass.
A hardcoded port collides with the platform's expected port and silently breaks routing.
identified_opportunities: A single PORT env var makes the same image portable across local, staging, and Maritime.
Startup address logging shortens debugging on the first deploy.

insights.insight: Idle sleep/wake makes cold-start behavior a contract requirement, so the health endpoint must be cheap and the warm path must be fast.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Maritime's public pages describe idle sleep and wake, so the first request after a quiet period lands on a cold process. If the health endpoint loads the model or warms caches, readiness checks and the first user request both stall, and the public URL looks broken. Separating a cheap /health that returns immediately from the heavier chat path lets the platform and users distinguish a waking container from a failed one. The team should also document expected wake latency and keep first-request work minimal, since Maritime hosts the lifecycle but the team owns what happens inside the process.
implementation_ideas: Implement /health to return 200 without loading the model, and load heavy resources lazily on the first chat request.
Document expected cold-start latency in the contract doc and surface a waking state in the chat response while the model loads.
Keep the first chat request cheap by deferring optional work and caching warm state after the first successful turn.
identified_risks: A heavy health check turns every wake into a timeout.
Lazy loading without a waking signal makes the first user request look like a hang.
identified_opportunities: A cheap health endpoint makes wake-up invisible to monitoring and users.
Documented cold-start behavior sets honest expectations and reduces support load.

insights.insight: The host/operate boundary should be drawn so Maritime owns the public runtime and routing, while the team owns the repository, image, and configuration, because that split follows what public pages can actually evidence.

Require the team to supply the image and config as deploy prerequisites owned by them.
Have Maritime's side limited to runtime hosting and public routing until a public page evidences more.

Block deployment until every row is either cited or explicitly accepted as an assumption by the team.
Record truncated or ambiguous source text verbatim next to the affected row.

Documenting token handling for headless CI as a first-class path, not a footnote to local login, removes the most common silent failure. Making branch selection an explicit, visible
experts.recommendation: Before the team deploys anything, have them produce a one-page pre-deploy prerequisites sheet built only from Maritime's public pages: account/tier requirement, API key or token creation step, the exact env var name and where it is stored (local .env vs CI secret), the branch/ref to deploy and whether that default is documented or inferred, and a two-column ownership split of platform-hosted versus team-operated items. Treat every cell marked 'inferred' as a question to confirm before the first public deploy, and run one dry deploy from CI, not a laptop, so token handling is proven headless be

insights.insight: The real onboarding cliff is the local-login-to-headless-CI transition, not account creation; teams need the token env var and CI secret step documented as its own path.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Account creation is usually a form; the failure point comes later, when a credential that worked interactively must be reproduced non-interactively in CI. If public pages only show the interactive flow, teams infer that the same token works headless, and the first CI run is where scope, env var naming, and secret storage assumptions surface — after the team believes onboarding is done. Mapping the exact prerequisite sequence and marking which steps are documented versus inferred exposes that cliff before deploy rather than during it.
implementation_ideas: Write a step-by-step prerequisite list that names the token env var explicitly and states whether it is created in the dashboard or CLI
Add a local-to-CI parity check: same env var name, secret stored in CI, one dry run from CI before any public deploy
Flag every prerequisite the public pages do not state as 'inferred — confirm' in the team's sheet
identified_risks: Token works locally but fails headless, and the team only learns at first CI run
Over-scoped token pasted into a public-facing deploy because scope is undocumented
identified_opportunities: A documented headless path shortens time-to-first-successful-CI-deploy
Explicit env var naming removes a whole class of silent misconfiguration

insights.insight: Branch/ref selection is an undocumented default waiting to deploy the wrong code; it must be an explicit, visible parameter with its default stated.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A team with an existing repository has multiple branches, and a public agent makes the deployed ref externally visible. If the public pages do not say which branch deploys or what the default is, the team infers main, or infers the current branch, and either guess can be wrong. Because branch choice sits in the pre-deploy prerequisite chain alongside account and token, it belongs on the same checklist and should be confirmed, not assumed, before the first public deploy.
implementation_ideas: Add 'branch/ref to deploy' as a required line on the prerequisites sheet with the chosen value written down
State whether the default branch is documented or inferred, and confirm it before deploy
Do one deploy from a non-default branch in staging to prove the selection actually takes effect
identified_risks: Wrong branch deployed to a public URL
Silent drift if the default ref changes and nobody re-checks
identified_opportunities: Explicit ref selection makes preview and production deploys separable
A written ref record gives an audit trail for what is public

insights.insight: Ownership must be split in writing before deploy: the platform hosts runtime, URL, and TLS; the team operates repo wiring, secrets, and agent config — and the public pages must be read for which is which.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The client question is precisely how Maritime should host the agent versus what the team runs. If that boundary is left to assumption, teams either expect the platform to cover secret management and branch discipline, or duplicate work the platform already does. Reading the public pages for an explicit hosting statement, and marking anything unstated as inferred, produces a two-column matrix the team can act on. This is the prerequisite that determines whether the other prerequisites are even the team's job.
implementation_ideas: Build a two-column sheet: platform-hosted items versus team-operated items, sourced only from public pages
Mark every ownership cell the pages do not state as 'inferred — confirm with Maritime'
Assign a named owner on the team for each team-operated row before the first deploy
identified_risks: Team assumes the platform manages secrets and ships an unmanaged token
Duplicated effort where the platform already hosts a capability
identified_opportunities: A written ownership split makes the public-agent decision reviewable
Clear boundaries reduce post-deploy surprises about who fixes what

experts.name: Ivo Tannenbaum
experts.background: Backend engineer who has built small HTTP wrappers around agents and reviewed two-endpoint service contracts; experienced with Dockerfile-at-root build conventions.
experts.lens: Checks whether the agent needs a chat contract or can ship as a plain web app, and specifies the minimal HTTP server, exposed port, and Dockerfile the team must produce before `maritime create` will s
experts.risks: The biggest contract risk is ambiguity about whether Maritime expects a chat-style agent endpoint (message in, message out, possibly streaming) or a plain web app (any HTTP server on a port). If the team guesses wrong, `maritime create` may succeed at build time but the deployed agent will not satisfy the platform's health or routing expectations. Second risk: Dockerfile-at-root conventions are easy to get subtly wrong (wrong base image, missing EXPOSE, binding to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0, no PORT env handling), producing a container that builds but is unreachable. Third: if the team alrea
experts.opportunities: A plain web-app contract is the lowest-friction path: one HTTP server, one exposed port, one Dockerfile at repo root, and the team keeps ownership of the agent logic, model calls, and secrets. This lets the team ship a public URL without adopting a chat protocol they do not need. It also gives a clean split of responsibilities: Maritime builds and hosts the container and routes traffic; the team operates the app, its dependencies, and its data. A minimal, documented contract also makes the artifact checklist reusable across future agents.
experts.recommendation: Ship as a plain web app, not a chat contract, unless public Maritime docs explicitly require a chat message schema. Require three artifacts before `maritime create`: (1) a Dockerfile at repository root that installs dependencies, copies the app, binds to 0.0.0.0, and honors a PORT environment variable with a sane default; (2) a single HTTP server exposing one port with a GET health endpoint returning 200 and one request-handling route; (3) a short CONTRACT.md stating the port, health path, request/response shape, and required env vars. The team operates the agent logic, model credentials, and

insights.insight: The agent should ship as a plain web app with one HTTP server and one exposed port, not a chat contract, unless Maritime's public docs mandate a message schema.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A public web agent needs an addressable HTTP surface, not necessarily a conversational protocol. A plain server keeps the contract small: one port, one health route, one handler. If Maritime later requires chat semantics, the handler can wrap the same logic. Choosing chat first adds schema and streaming work the team may not need, and a wrong guess is costlier than a thin HTTP layer.
implementation_ideas: Write a single-file server (e.g., Python http.server or a small Node/Express app) with GET /health returning 200 and POST /agent returning JSON.
Read the port from a PORT env var, default to 8080, and bind to 0.0.0.0.
Document the request/response JSON in CONTRACT.md so the shape is explicit before deploy.
identified_risks: Maritime may expect a chat message schema and reject a generic handler.
A generic POST route can hide input-validation gaps.
identified_opportunities: Reuse the same server as a local dev harness.
Swap in a chat adapter later without rewriting the agent.

insights.insight: A Dockerfile at repository root is a hard prerequisite, and its correctness (base image, 0.0.0.0 binding, PORT handling, EXPOSE) matters more than its brevity.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Build conventions at repo root are what a platform like Maritime will look for; a Dockerfile in a subdirectory or a missing one blocks `maritime create`. The common failure is a container that builds but is unreachable because the process binds to localhost or ignores PORT. Pinning a base image and documenting the exposed port makes the build reproducible and the runtime predictable.
implementation_ideas: Commit a Dockerfile at repo root using a pinned slim base image, installing only runtime dependencies.
Add EXPOSE matching the default port and ensure the entrypoint binds 0.0.0.0:$PORT.
Build and run the image locally, curl /health on the mapped port, and only then run `maritime create`.
identified_risks: Localhost binding yields a healthy build but unreachable service.
Unpinned base images drift between builds.
identified_opportunities: A verified local image run catches most deploy failures early.
The same Dockerfile works for local and hosted runs.

insights.insight: Responsibility should split cleanly: the team operates agent logic, credentials, and data; Maritime operates build, hosting, and public routing. The contract must state this so neither side assumes the other's job.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The team already has a repo, so they own the code and its dependencies. Maritime's value is turning that repo into a public URL. Without an explicit split, the team may expect Maritime to manage secrets or model keys, or Maritime may assume the app self-heals. Writing the split into CONTRACT.md and the artifact checklist prevents scope gaps at deploy time.
implementation_ideas: List required env vars (model key, config) in CONTRACT.md and inject them at runtime, never baking secrets into the image.
State in CONTRACT.md that the team owns uptime of the agent logic and external calls; Maritime owns container hosting and routing.
Add a startup check that fails fast with a clear log line if a required env var is missing.
identified_risks: Secrets baked into the image leak via layers.
Unclear ownership leaves health monitoring unassigned.
identified_opportunities: Explicit ownership shortens incident triage.
Fail-fast startup checks make misconfiguration obvious.

experts.name: Naledi Frost-Quintero
experts.background: Reviews public documentation for claims that could be mistaken for vendor endorsement; tracks source provenance and assumption labeling in technical write-ups.
experts.lens: Ensures every statement traces to a public maritime.sh page, marks truncated or assumed details (like the `--port` default), and keeps the work framed as independent public-source research.
experts.risks: Public maritime.sh pages are the only admissible evidence, and the client's question (how should Maritime host the agent, what does the team operate, what artifacts precede deployment) is a hosting/architecture question that public marketing pages may not answer at the level of detail needed. The main risks are: (1) provenance drift — a reviewer or the client later reads a claim that cannot be traced to a specific public page, or that was true of a different page than cited; (2) silent assumption-filling — most acutely the `--port` default and any CLI flag semantics, which are easy to state as
experts.opportunities: A provenance-first write-up gives the client something more durable than a vendor pitch: a claim-by-claim map of what public sources actually establish, with gaps marked as gaps. That makes the hosting/operated-by-whom split auditable and lets the client re-check every line against the cited page. Labeling assumptions (especially CLI defaults like `--port`) turns hidden guesswork into reviewable decisions the team can confirm before deploy. Framing the work as independent public-source research protects the client from over-reading a marketing page as a commitment, and gives Maritime-facing co
experts.recommendation: Produce a short, citation-per-line public-source brief before any hosting decision: one table of claims (each with the exact maritime.sh URL and retrieval date), one column marking each claim as stated / truncated / assumed, and an explicit 'not established by public sources' list covering the hosting split and the `--port` default. Present the hosting model and the team-operated surface as a proposed split conditioned on those citations, not as Maritime's stated design, and state up front that this is independent research, not commissioned work. Hold the artifact checklist to items the public

insights.insight: Every hosting and responsibility claim should carry a page-level citation and a status tag (stated, truncated, assumed), because the client's decision hinges on details public pages may only partially cover.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The client is deciding what Maritime hosts versus what the team operates — a split that public marketing pages often describe only in outline. Without a per-claim status tag, a reader cannot tell a documented capability from a reviewer's inference, and the `--port` default is the clearest example of a detail likely to be assumed rather than published. Tagging makes the weak points visible and reviewable instead of buried in fluent prose. It also enforces the independent-research framing, since a cited table reads as research while uncited prose reads as endorsement.
implementation_ideas: Build a three-column claim table: claim text, exact maritime.sh URL plus retrieval date, status tag (stated / truncated / assumed).
Add a standing rule that any sentence about hosting, operated-by-whom, or CLI flags without a 'stated' tag is rewritten as 'assumed — confirm with Maritime'.
Include a short methods note at the top stating the brief is independent public-source research and not commissioned by Maritime.
identified_risks: A page may change or be taken down after retrieval, breaking citations the client relies on.
Status tags can be dropped when the brief is summarized for stakeholders, restoring the original ambiguity.
identified_opportunities: The tagged table becomes a reusable audit artifact the client can re-verify before deploy.
Visible assumption tags give the client a precise question list for Maritime rather than vague uncertainty.

insights.insight: The `--port` default and similar CLI flag semantics must be marked assumed unless a public page states them, and the deployment artifacts list should be split into 'public-source-supported' and 'team-confirmed' buckets.
insights.supporting_reasoning: CLI defaults are exactly the kind of detail that gets filled in from familiarity and then hardens into false fact. The client needs artifacts before deploy, but public pages may establish only some of them; mixing supported and unsupported items in one list implies uniform evidence. Splitting the list preserves the useful output while keeping provenance honest, and it maps directly onto the hosting question: artifacts the team must own are precisely the ones public sources do not settle. This keeps the reviewer's lens — traceability and assumption labeling — applied to the deliverable the client will actually act on.
implementation_ideas: Create two artifact lists side by side: 'supported by public page (cited)' and 'team-confirmed before deploy (assumed)'.
For each CLI flag mentioned, including `--port`, write the assumed default in brackets with a 'verify' marker rather than stating it plainly.
Add a one-line pre-deploy gate: no assumed item ships until the team records who confirmed it and on what date.
identified_risks: An assumed default repeated often enough may be read as documented fact by later readers.
The team-confirmed bucket can become a dumping ground that is never actually confirmed.
identified_opportunities: The split list doubles as the team's own pre-deployment checklist.
Bracketed assumptions make the brief safe to circulate widely without overclaiming.

insights.insight: The hosting model should be presented as a proposed split conditioned on citations, with an explicit 'not established by public sources' section, rather than as Maritime's documented design.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The client asked how Maritime should host the agent and what the team operates — a normative question, while public pages are descriptive and possibly incomplete. Presenting a proposal as documented design is the most likely source of endorsement confusion. A dedicated 'not established' section absorbs the gaps honestly and gives the client a bounded list to close with Maritime. This also keeps the independent-research frame intact: the brief proposes, the public pages support, and the client decides.
implementation_ideas: Open the hosting section with 'Proposed split (conditioned on cited pages)' and close it with a 'Not established by public sources' subsection.
For each proposed responsibility, name the cited page that supports it or mark it 'proposal only'.
Route every 'not established' item into a numbered open-questions list addressed to the client, not answered in the brief.
identified_risks: A proposal section may still be skimmed as Maritime's own recommendation.
The 'not established' list could grow large enough to make the brief look thin.
identified_opportunities: The open-questions list gives the client a ready agenda for a Maritime conversation.
Honest gap-marking builds reviewer credibility and reduces later correction work.

experts.name: Bastian Quill-Nakamura
experts.background: Technical writer who turns architecture findings into ordered pre-deploy checklists and artifact inventories for engineering teams.
experts.lens: Synthesizes the split of responsibilities into a concrete artifact list — root Dockerfile, chosen branch, exposed port, account/API key, `MARITIME_TOKEN` for CI — and sequences them before the `--publ
experts.risks: Public pages alone may not pin down Maritime's exact deploy contract (CLI flags, env var names, branch conventions), so a checklist built from them risks being subtly wrong at the exact step where teams fail. The `MARITIME_TOKEN` and `--publ` sequence is inferred from the prompt's framing, not verified against docs, so ordering could mislead. Teams may assume Maritime hosts more than it does (build, secrets, runtime ops) and arrive without a root Dockerfile or a chosen branch, stalling at intake. A public web agent also exposes an attack surface the team must own, and a checklist that treats e
experts.opportunities: A sequenced artifact inventory turns a vague 'make it public' request into a short, checkable pre-deploy gate that shortens time-to-first-deploy and reduces support load. Making the responsibility split explicit (team owns repo, Dockerfile, branch, port, account/API key, CI token; Maritime owns hosting and public exposure) sets expectations before the `--publ` step. The same inventory doubles as onboarding documentation and a review artifact. Clear ownership also improves the security posture of the exposed agent by forcing the team to name the port and key handling up front.
experts.recommendation: Ship a single ordered pre-deploy checklist that gates the `--publ` step: (1) root-level Dockerfile committed, (2) deploy branch chosen and named, (3) exposed port declared, (4) account and API key provisioned, (5) `MARITIME_TOKEN` set in CI. State the split plainly — the team operates the repo, image, branch, port, credentials, and CI; Maritime hosts and exposes the agent publicly — and require every artifact to be checked before `--publ` runs.

insights.insight: The artifact list is the real deliverable; the hosting decision is downstream of it.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The client already has a repository, so the open question is not whether to build but what must exist before a public deploy. Each artifact maps to a failure mode: no root Dockerfile means no buildable image; no chosen branch means an ambiguous deploy target; no declared port means the agent cannot be reached; no account/API key means no authenticated runtime; no `MARITIME_TOKEN` means CI cannot trigger the deploy. Sequencing them before `--publ` converts tacit knowledge into a gate. This is a synthesis from the problem framing, not from verified docs.
implementation_ideas: Publish the checklist as a numbered gate with a one-line 'why' per item
Mark each item pass/fail in the PR template so review blocks `--publ` until green
Keep the list in the repo root next to the Dockerfile so it travels with the code
identified_risks: Item names may drift from actual CLI/env conventions
Teams may treat the checklist as optional ceremony
identified_opportunities: Reuse the checklist as onboarding docs
Cut support tickets caused by missing artifacts

insights.insight: The responsibility split must be written down, not assumed, or teams will expect Maritime to own build and secrets.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Hosting a public agent splits into two halves: what the team operates (repo, root Dockerfile, branch, port, account/API key, `MARITIME_TOKEN` in CI) and what Maritime does (host and expose publicly). Without an explicit split, teams arrive expecting Maritime to author the Dockerfile or manage keys, and the `--publ` step fails on missing inputs. Writing the split into the checklist makes each side's obligations checkable and puts credential handling with the party that owns the account.
implementation_ideas: Add an 'Owned by: team / Maritime' column to every checklist row
State the split in one paragraph above the checklist
Require a named owner per artifact before `--publ`
identified_risks: Overlap or gaps if the split is read as exhaustive when it is not
Teams may still assume Maritime handles key rotation
identified_opportunities: Fewer mis-scoped requests at intake
Clearer security ownership for the exposed agent

insights.insight: Ordering matters more than completeness: credentials and the CI token belong after the build artifacts, immediately before `--publ`.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A Dockerfile, branch, and port can be prepared and reviewed without secrets; the account/API key and `MARITIME_TOKEN` are only needed when CI triggers the public deploy. Sequencing build artifacts first lets review happen before credentials are live, and placing the token last means it is set only when everything else is green. This reduces the window in which a token exists for a deploy that cannot succeed.
implementation_ideas: Number the checklist so token setup is the final pre-`--publ` step
Gate `--publ` on all prior items passing
Document token scope as deploy-trigger only
identified_risks: Exact ordering is inferred, not verified against docs
Late token setup can surprise teams that expected it first
identified_opportunities: Shorter credential exposure window
Review happens before secrets are provisioned

top5.title: Ship a committed, provenance-tagged deploy manifest that declares the platform/team seam
top5.detail: Before any public deploy, the team commits a single deploy manifest to the repo that names, in two explicit columns, what Maritime hosts (build execution, runtime, routing, TLS, sleep/wake, log capture, public URL) and what the team operates (repo, Dockerfile, entrypoint, port/env contract, health endpoint, secrets, auth/rate-limit layer, domain). top5.rationale: This is the round's convergent position: Voss's seam-declaration frame survived, but Reingold, Frost-Quintero, Brandvold and Osei-Blackwood all forced provenance tagging because the public text is truncated on --port and silent on scaling/logs/rollback. skills.description: Drafts a committed, provenance-tagged deploy manifest that declares the Maritime-hosted vs. team-operated seam before any public deploy. Use when a team with an existing repository is preparing to host a public web agent on Maritime and needs the hosting split written down and approved.
skills.instructions:
# Deploy Manifest (Hosting Seam)

## Overview
Before a public deploy, the team commits one deploy manifest to the repo that names, in two explicit columns, what Maritime hosts and what the team operates. This makes the seam auditable and prevents silent assumptions about who owns runtime, routing, and abuse exposure. The manifest is provenance-tagged with the source of each claim.

## When to use
- A team has a repo and wants a public web agent but has not yet declared the hosting split.
- A reviewer asks "who operates what" before `--public` is flipped.
- The repo lacks a single artifact describing the platform/team boundary.

## Inputs
- Repository tree and existing Dockerfile/entrypoint (if any).
- Maritime public docs and pricing pages (cite URLs).
- Team's stated runtime, port, and env contract.

## Steps
1. Read the repo and list every deploy-relevant artifact present or missing.
2. Fill the two-column manifest using `manifest-template.md`: left column = Maritime-hosted (build execution, runtime, routing, TLS, sleep/wake, log capture, public URL); right column = team-operated (repo, Dockerfile, entrypoint, port/env contract, health endpoint, rate limiter, secrets).
3. Tag each row with provenance: `docs:<url>`, `repo:<path>`, or `assumption` (flag assumptions for human confirmation).
4. Mark any row where ownership is ambiguous and propose a default.
5. Write `deploy-manifest.md` at repo root and open a PR.
6. Require human approval on the seam before the first public deploy.

## Output format
A committed `deploy-manifest.md` with two columns, a provenance tag per row, and an "Open questions" section. PR description summarizes the split in five lines.

## Guardrails
- Do not invent Maritime capabilities; cite public pages only.
- Do not claim the company commissioned this work.
- Never mark a row `docs:` without a real URL.
- Do not flip `--public` in this skill.

## Example
Team-operated row: `health endpoint | repo:app/server.py | team`. Maritime-hosted row: `TLS termination | docs:https://maritime.sh/docs | platform`. Ambiguous row flagged: `sleep/wake budget | assumption | confirm with Maritime docs`.

skills.name: maritime-predeploy-gate

skills.instructions:
# Pre-Deploy Artifact Gate

## Overview
A human-read checklist gets skipped. This skill turns the ordered pre-deploy checklist into a pipeline gate that fails closed: each artifact is checked in order and the pipeline stops at the first failure.

## When to use
- The repo has a deploy manifest and is approaching first public deploy.
- The team wants CI to enforce artifacts instead of relying on review.
- A previous deploy failed for a missing artifact.

## Inputs
- Repo tree, Dockerfile, lockfile, `.dockerignore`, `CONTRACT.md`.
- CI config location.

## Steps
1. Load `checklist.md`; it is the ordered, authoritative list.
2. For each item in order, write a CI step that exits non-zero on failure.
3. Enforce: root Dockerfile with digest-pinned base image; committed lockfile; `.dockerignore` excluding `.git`, `.env`, test fixtures; declared `EXPOSE` matching the actual listener; `GET /health` returning 200; `CONTRACT.md` present.
4. Wire the gate to run on every PR and block merge on failure.
5. Run the gate locally once and paste output into the PR.
6. Only after a green gate may the deploy step run.

## Output format
A CI job named `predeploy-gate` with ordered steps mirroring `checklist.md`, plus a PR comment showing a green local run.

## Guardrails
- Fail closed: missing item = non-zero exit, never a warning.
- Do not reorder checklist items.
- Do not auto-fix secrets; only flag them.
- Cite public docs for any Maritime-specific claim.

## Example
Step 4 fails because `EXPOSE 8080` does not match listener on `PORT` (default 3000). Gate exits 1; deploy blocked until fixed.
skills.helper_content:

Run in order. Stop at first failure.

1. Root-level `Dockerfile` exists.
2. Base image is digest-pinned (`FROM x@sha256:...`).
3. Lockfile committed.
4. `.dockerignore` excludes `.git`, `.env`, test fixtures.
5. `EXPOSE` port matches the actual listener.
6. `GET /health` returns 200.
7. `CONTRACT.md` present and complete.
8. Rate limiter and input validator present at the edge.
9. Max-wake budget documented.
10. Idle-sleep configuration set deliberately.

skills.instructions:
# Agent Contract and Edge Controls

## Overview
Default the agent to a plain web app: one HTTP server bound to `0.0.0.0` on a single `PORT`-configurable port, a `GET /health` returning 200, and one request-handling route. Commit a short `CONTRACT.md`. Add an app-level rate limiter and input validator at the edge before `--public`, because public exposure shifts abuse and cost to the team.

## When to use
- The repo has no server entrypoint or an unclear one.
- The team is about to flip `--public` and needs abuse/cost controls.
- A conversational agent needs a chat contract decision.

## Inputs
- Language/runtime of the repo.
- Whether the agent is conversational.
- Env vars required.

## Steps
1. Run the one-question classifier: is the agent conversational? If no, use the plain HTTP contract only. If yes, add a chat contract section.
2. Scaffold one server bound to `0.0.0.0:$PORT` with `GET /health` -> 200 and one handler route.
3. Add a per-IP rate limiter and an input validator at the edge.
4. Document a max-wake budget and deliberate idle-sleep setting.
5. Fill `CONTRACT.md` from the template: port, health path, request/response shape, required env vars.
6. Add `.env.example`; never commit real secrets.
7. Smoke-test locally: health 200, handler responds, limiter returns 429 past threshold.

## Output format
Server file(s), `CONTRACT.md`, `.env.example`, and a smoke-test log showing health, handler, and 429 behavior.

## Guardrails
- Single port only; bind `0.0.0.0`.
- Health must be unauthenticated and always 200 when up.
- Do not commit secrets.
- Do not claim Maritime-specific behavior without a public citation.

## Example
`GET /health` -> `200 ok`. `POST /run` with valid body -> 200. 61st request in a minute from one IP -> `429`.

kit_files.harness:
## Purpose

This document specifies a harness design for an agent system that delivers the Top 5 outcomes for a software team that already has a repository and wants Maritime (maritime.sh) to host a public web agent. The harness coordinates discovery, repository audit, hosting-shape decision, artifact generation, public deploy, and post-deploy operation. It is designed around public information about Maritime only; no customer names, metrics, or quotes are asserted. All numeric expectations are labeled **targets**.

The harness exists to make the platform/team seam explicit, make the first public deploy fail closed on missing artifacts, force a plain single-port HTTP contract, put abuse and cost controls in the team's container before `--public`, and publish one provenance-carrying access and artifact page.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    U[Team operator] --> O[Orchestrator agent]
    O --> D[Discovery agent]
    O --> A[Repo audit agent]
    O --> H[Hosting-shape agent]
    O --> P[Artifact prep agent]
    O --> S[Deploy and smoke-test agent]
    O --> R[Operate and iterate agent]

    D --> MCP1[MCP: docs-crawler]
    A --> MCP2[MCP: repo-scanner]
    A --> MCP3[MCP: secret-scanner]
    P --> MCP4[MCP: artifact-writer]
    P --> MCP5[MCP: contract-linter]
    S --> MCP6[MCP: maritime-cli]
    S --> MCP7[MCP: public-smoke]
    R --> MCP8[MCP: log-tail]
    R --> MCP9[MCP: uptime-probe]
    R --> MCP10[MCP: pr-opener]

    O --> ST[(State store)]
    O --> G{Gate: predeploy}
    G -->|pass| S
    G -->|fail| P
    O --> Q[QHX delta writer]
    Q --> AP[(Anti-pattern list)]
    AP --> O
```

The orchestrator is the only agent that mutates state transitions. Sub-agents are single-purpose and return structured results. The predeploy gate is a hard edge: the deploy agent cannot run until the gate returns pass. Every production run terminates by writing exactly one QHX delta.

## Agents and roles

| Agent | Type | Responsibility | Inputs | Outputs | Human checkpoint |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator | AI | Sequences stages, owns state transitions, enforces gate | Run request, state store | Stage assignments, final report | None (supervised) |
| Discovery | AI | Crawls public maritime.sh docs and pricing, extracts hosting primitives | Public URLs | Capability brief | None |
| Repo audit | Hybrid | Scans repo for entrypoints, secrets, build steps; proposes manifest skeleton | Repo snapshot | Audit report, manifest draft | Confirms secret findings |
| Hosting-shape | Hybrid | Recommends Maritime-hosted vs team-operated vs hybrid split | Capability brief, audit report | Seam decision record | **Approves tradeoffs** |
| Artifact prep | Hybrid | Generates Dockerfile, CONTRACT.md, env manifest, health check, README, rate limiter | Seam decision, audit report | Artifact PR | **Reviews secrets and public exposure** |
| Deploy and smoke-test | Hybrid | Runs predeploy gate, triggers deploy, runs public smoke tests | Passing gate, artifact PR | Live URL, smoke report | **Signs off on live URL** |
| Operate and iterate | Hybrid | Monitors logs and uptime, opens fix PRs | Live URL, log stream | Fix PRs, incident notes | Owns incident response and policy changes |

## Tools and MCP servers

- `docs-crawler` — fetches and extracts public maritime.sh pages; read-only, cached per run.
- `repo-scanner` — walks the repository tree, detects entrypoints, Dockerfiles, lockfiles, `.dockerignore`, `EXPOSE`, and listener bindings.
- `secret-scanner` — detects committed secrets and `.env` leakage; blocks on high-confidence findings.
- `artifact-writer` — writes files to a branch and opens a PR; never pushes to the default branch.
- `contract-linter` — validates `CONTRACT.md` against the actual listener, port, and health path.
- `maritime-cli` — wraps deploy, `--public` flip, and sleep/wake configuration; requires `MARITIME_TOKEN` in CI.
- `public-smoke` — issues unauthenticated requests to the live URL: `GET /health` expects 200, one request route expects a valid response shape.
- `log-tail` — streams captured logs post-deploy.
- `uptime-probe` — periodic external probe with alert threshold.
- `pr-opener` — opens fix PRs from operate stage.

All MCP servers are scoped to least privilege. `maritime-cli` is the only server with write access to the platform.

## Skills

- **maritime-deploy-manifest** — produces the committed, provenance-tagged deploy manifest with two explicit columns: what Maritime hosts (build execution, runtime, routing, TLS, sleep/wake, log capture, public URL) and what the team operates (repo, Dockerfile, entrypoint, port/env contract, health endpoint, rate limiter, idle-sleep policy). Every manifest line carries a provenance tag pointing to the public source or repo path that justifies it.
- **maritime-predeploy-gate** — converts the ordered checklist into a CI-enforced, fail-closed gate. Required in order: root-level Dockerfile with digest-pinned base image; committed lockfile; `.dockerignore` excluding `.git`, `.env`, test fixtures; declared `EXPOSE` matching the actual listener; `GET /health` returning 200; `CONTRACT.md` present and lint-clean; app-level rate limiter and input validator present; documented max-wake budget; deliberate idle-sleep configuration. Any missing item fails the gate with a named reason.
- **maritime-agent-contract** — enforces the plain single-port HTTP default: one server bound to `0.0.0.0` on a single `PORT`-configurable port, one request-handling route, and a chat contract only if the agent is conversational. Runs the one-question classifier to decide chat vs plain and records the decision in `CONTRACT.md`.

## State schema

```yaml
run_id: string
repo: {url: string, default_branch: string, commit: string}
stage: enum[discover, audit, shape, prepare, gate, deploy, operate, done, failed]
capability_brief: {primitives: [string], sources: [url]}
audit: {entrypoints: [string], secrets: [finding], build_steps: [string]}
seam_decision: {hosted: [string], operated: [string], approved_by: string, approved_at: ts}
artifacts: {dockerfile: path, contract_md: path, env_manifest: path, health: path, rate_limiter: path, pr_url: string}
gate: {status: enum[pending, pass, fail], failures: [string], checked_at: ts}
deploy: {public: bool, url: string, smoke: {health_status: int, route_status: int, passed: bool}}
operate: {log_cursor: string, uptime_state: enum[up, down], open_prs: [string]}
qhx_delta: {anti_pattern_id: string, evidence: string, proposed_change: string}
```

State is append-only per stage; transitions are validated by the orchestrator against the stage enum.

## Workflow

1. **Discover** — Discovery agent crawls public maritime.sh docs and pricing and drafts a capability brief. No repo access yet.
2. **Audit** — Repo audit agent scans the repository, flags missing entrypoints, secrets, and build steps, and proposes a manifest skeleton. Human confirms secret findings.
3. **Choose shape** — Hosting-shape agent recommends hosted vs team-operated vs hybrid split and writes the seam decision record. **Human approves tradeoffs.**
4. **Prepare artifacts** — Artifact prep agent generates Dockerfile, `CONTRACT.md`, env manifest, health check, README, and rate limiter, then opens a PR. **Human reviews secrets and public exposure.**
5. **Gate** — `maritime-predeploy-gate` runs in CI. Fail closed: any missing artifact returns to stage 4 with named failures.
6. **Deploy and smoke-test** — Deploy agent flips `--public` only after gate pass, triggers deploy, and runs public smoke tests. **Human signs off on the live URL.**
7. **Operate and iterate** — Operate agent monitors logs and uptime and opens fix PRs. Humans own incident response and policy changes.
8. **Close** — Orchestrator writes exactly one QHX delta to the anti-pattern list and emits the run report.

## Guardrails and anti-patterns

Guardrails:
- Gate is fail-closed; no manual override without a recorded reason in state.
- `--public` is flipped only by the deploy agent after gate pass and human sign-off.
- No secret values in logs; secret-scanner blocks high-confidence findings.
- Artifact writer never pushes to the default branch.
- Rate limiter and input validator must exist in the team's container before `--public`; per-IP throttling, max-wake budget, and idle-sleep configuration are gate items.
- One provenance tag per manifest line; untagged lines fail lint.
- Chat contract only if the classifier says conversational.

Anti-patterns (seeded list, extended by QHX):
- AP-001: Deploying with a floating base image tag.
- AP-002: `EXPOSE` port that does not match the listener.
- AP-003: Health endpoint that returns 200 without checking dependencies.
- AP-004: Flipping `--public` before the rate limiter ships.
- AP-005: Two onboarding documents that teams must reconcile.
- AP-006: Email verification or trial card demanded before the create command is previewed.
- AP-007: Chat contract bolted onto a non-conversational agent.
- AP-008: Undocumented max-wake budget allowing wake-on-visit cost drift.

## Evals

**Offline**
- Gate fixture suite: seeded repos with each missing artifact; gate must fail with the correct named reason. Pass criterion: 100% of fixtures fail correctly and zero false passes.
- Contract linter suite: mismatched port, missing health path, chat contract on plain agent. Pass criterion: all mismatches flagged.
- Manifest lint: untagged lines rejected. Pass criterion: 100% rejection.
- Classifier suite: labeled plain vs conversational cases. **Target:** ≥95% agreement with labels.

**Online**
- Public smoke on every deploy: `GET /health` returns 200 and the request route returns the documented shape. Pass criterion: both pass before sign-off.
- Rate limiter probe: burst above threshold returns 429. Pass criterion: 429 observed within the documented window.
- Uptime probe: alert fires within the configured threshold on simulated downtime. **Target:** alert latency under 2 minutes.
- QHX delta presence: every production run writes exactly one delta. Pass criterion: 100% of runs.

## QHX improvement loop

Every production run writes exactly one delta to the anti-pattern list before the run closes. A delta contains the anti-pattern id (existing or new), the evidence from the run, and a proposed change to a skill, gate item, or guardrail. Deltas are reviewed on a fixed cadence; accepted deltas update the seeded anti-pattern list and, where relevant, the gate fixture suite. The orchestrator reads the current anti-pattern list at run start so new entries take effect immediately. A run that cannot produce a delta is marked incomplete.

## Rollout plan (30/60/90 days)

**Days 0–30** — Stand up orchestrator, discovery, and repo audit. Ship `maritime-deploy-manifest` and the manifest lint. Seed the anti-pattern list. Run offline gate fixtures in shadow mode. **Target:** gate fixtures at 100% correct failure.

**Days 31–60** — Enable hosting-shape and artifact prep with human checkpoints. Turn on the predeploy gate as a required CI check. Ship `maritime-agent-contract` and the classifier suite. Begin online smoke and rate limiter probes. **Target:** classifier agreement ≥95%; zero false gate passes.

**Days 61–90** — Enable deploy, smoke-test, and operate stages with human sign-off. Turn on QHX delta enforcement and the review cadence. Publish the single provenance-carrying access and artifact page, GitHub-first, with browser-code CLI login for humans and `MARITIME_TOKEN` for CI. **Target:** 100% of production runs carry a QHX delta; one page replaces the two onboarding documents.
